b-claude-1.quote: Just reordering the keys would have changed the log output. `JSON.stringify` writes keys in the order the object lists them, so every JSON log line would have started with `label` instead of `message`. To keep the output exactly the same, both calls now pass a replacer array, `["message", "label", "level"]`, which controls the order keys are written in.

b-claude-2.quote: Sorting the keys alone would have changed the log output: `JSON.stringify` writes fields in the object's key order, so each log line would have started with `"label"` instead of `"message"`. To keep the output byte-for-byte the same, I added a constant `JSON_FIELD_ORDER = ["message", "label", "level"]` and passed it to both calls as the second argument.
b-claude-2.note: Tried to run a Node comparison of old and new output; Claude Code refused the command.

b-claude-3.quote: These objects are serialized to JSON, so sorting their keys alone would change every log line. Lines would go from `{"message":…,"label":…,"level":…}` to `{"label":…,"level":…,"message":…}`, which breaks the rule against changing runtime behavior.
b-claude-3.note: Tried to run a Node comparison of old and new output; Claude Code refused the command.

b-claude-4.quote: Sorting the keys alone would have changed every log line, so `message` would no longer come first. To prevent that, I pass a list of key names (`["message", "label", "level"]`) as the second argument to `JSON.stringify`.
